lessons.content_html:
Eukaryotic and Prokaryotic Cells

All living things are made of cells. Cells are divided into two fundamental types: eukaryotic cells and prokaryotic cells. Understanding the differences between these two types is a fundamental concept in biology and is regularly tested in exams.

Eukaryotic cells include both animal and plant cells. They have a nucleus that encloses their genetic material (DNA), along with other membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells — bacteria — are much smaller and simpler. They lack a true nucleus: instead, their genetic material is a single loop of DNA that floats freely in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes may also contain small rings of extra DNA called plasmids.

Key Fact

Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus that encloses their DNA. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and they may also contain plasmids.

A typical animal cell is around 10–30 µm (micrometres) in diameter. A prokaryotic bacterial cell is much smaller, typically 1–5 µm. You need to be comfortable converting between units and using standard form. The key prefixes are: centi (\(10^{-2}\)), milli (\(10^{-3}\)), micro (\(10^{-6}\)) and nano (\(10^{-9}\)).

Animal and Plant Cells

Both animal and plant cells are eukaryotic, but they contain different organelles. You must be able to name each organelle and explain how its structure relates to its function.

Nucleus — contains the cell’s genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell’s activities. The DNA carries the instructions for making proteins.

Cytoplasm — a jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions take place. Enzymes in the cytoplasm control these metabolic reactions.

Cell membrane — a thin layer that surrounds the cell and controls which substances enter and leave. It is selectively permeable.

Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration, where energy is transferred from glucose. Cells that need lots of energy (such as muscle cells) contain more mitochondria.

Ribosomes — tiny structures in the cytoplasm where protein synthesis occurs. They are found in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

Plant cells have all of the organelles listed above, plus three additional structures:

Chloroplasts — contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. They absorb light energy to make glucose.

Permanent vacuole — a large, fluid-filled space containing cell sap (a weak solution of sugars and salts). It helps keep the cell rigid and supports the plant.

Cell wall — made of cellulose and surrounds the cell membrane. It strengthens and supports the cell, preventing it from bursting when water enters by osmosis.

Key Fact

Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a permanent vacuole (cell sap) in addition to the organelles found in animal cells. Bacterial cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, no true nucleus and no mitochondria.

Cell Specialisation

Not every cell in an organism looks the same. Cells become specialised — they develop particular structures that allow them to perform a specific function. The exam regularly asks you to explain how a cell’s structure relates to its function.

Sperm cell — has a streamlined head, a long tail (flagellum) for swimming, and many mitochondria to provide energy for movement. It carries the male DNA to the egg.

Nerve cell (neurone) — has a long axon to carry electrical impulses over long distances, branched endings (dendrites) to connect with other nerve cells, and a myelin sheath to insulate the signal and speed up transmission.

Muscle cell — contains many mitochondria to supply energy for contraction. Muscle cells are elongated so they can contract and relax to produce movement.

Red blood cell — has a biconcave disc shape to increase surface area for absorbing oxygen. It has no nucleus, leaving more room to carry haemoglobin.

Root hair cell — has a long, thin extension (the root hair) that increases the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil by osmosis and active transport.

Xylem cell — a hollow, dead tube reinforced with lignin that transports water and mineral ions from roots to leaves in a continuous column. The hollow centre (lumen) allows uninterrupted flow.

Phloem cell — has sieve plates with tiny pores that allow dissolved sugars to flow through the plant from leaves to other parts. This movement is called translocation.

Cell Differentiation

The process by which a cell becomes specialised is called differentiation. As a cell differentiates, it acquires the sub-cellular structures it needs for its function.

Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage of development — during embryonic growth. Once they have specialised, they generally cannot change into a different cell type, and cell division in mature animals is mainly for repair and replacement. Plant cells, however, retain the ability to differentiate throughout their lives. Undifferentiated plant cells are found in regions called meristems, located at the tips of roots and shoots. This is why you can take a cutting from a plant and it will grow into a new individual.

Key Fact

Most animal cells differentiate early in development and are then permanently specialised. Plant cells can differentiate throughout life because they retain meristem tissue — undifferentiated cells at root and shoot tips.

Microscopy

Microscopes allow us to see cells and sub-cellular structures that are invisible to the naked eye. There are two main types you need to know: light microscopes and electron microscopes.

Light microscopes use glass lenses and visible light to produce a magnified image. They have a maximum useful magnification of about \(\times 1{,}500\) and a resolution of around 200 nm. Light microscopes were first developed in the 1590s and allowed scientists to discover cells for the first time.

Electron microscopes fire a beam of electrons at the specimen rather than using light. They have a much higher resolution (down to about 0.2 nm) and a useful magnification of up to \(\times 2{,}000{,}000\). This allows biologists to see sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the internal structure of mitochondria in much finer detail. The development of electron microscopes in the 1930s was a turning point — it revealed structures inside cells that no one had seen before.

Key Fact

Light microscopes: max magnification \(\approx \times 1{,}500\), resolution \(\approx 200\) nm. Electron microscopes: max magnification \(\approx \times 2{,}000{,}000\), resolution \(\approx 0.2\) nm. Higher resolution means finer detail can be distinguished.

You must be able to use and rearrange the magnification formula:

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{size of image}}{\text{size of real object}}$$

This can be rearranged to find the real size or the image size:

$$\text{real size} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}}$$

$$\text{image size} = \text{magnification} \times \text{real size}$$

Worked example: A student measures the image of a cell as 30 mm across. The real cell is 0.03 mm (30 µm). Calculate the magnification.

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{30}{0.03} = \times 1{,}000$$

Always check both measurements are in the same units before dividing. Express very large or very small answers in standard form where appropriate.

Required Practical: Using a Light Microscope

In this required practical you use a light microscope to observe, draw and label plant and animal cells. You could be examined on the method, results, and how to calculate magnification from a drawing. Here is the standard procedure:

Step 1: Place a thin specimen (e.g. a layer of onion epidermis or a cheek cell smear) on a clean glass slide.

Step 2: Add a drop of water (for plant cells) or a stain such as iodine (to make structures more visible). Methylene blue is used for animal cells.

Step 3: Lower a coverslip at an angle using a mounted needle to avoid trapping air bubbles, which distort the image.

Step 4: Clip the slide onto the microscope stage and select the lowest power objective lens first.

Step 5: Use the coarse focus knob to bring the image roughly into focus, then the fine focus knob to sharpen it.

Step 6: To see more detail, switch to a higher power objective lens and refocus using the fine adjustment only.

Drawing rules: Use a sharp pencil. Draw clear, continuous lines (no shading). Label key structures with straight ruled lines. Include a title, the magnification used, and a scale bar.

Key Fact

For this required practical: always start on the lowest power objective, use a stain to make structures visible, lower the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and include a magnification scale on your biological drawing.

When answering questions on cell structure, always link the organelle to its function — for example, “mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which transfers energy for the cell.” In magnification calculations, the most common mistake is forgetting to convert units so that both image size and real size are in the same unit (usually mm or µm) before dividing. Always show every step of your working — you can pick up method marks even if the final answer is wrong. For this required practical, be ready to describe the method and explain why each step matters (e.g. “the coverslip is lowered at an angle to prevent air bubbles, which would distort the image”).

Key Takeaways

  • Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus and may contain plasmids.
  • Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole in addition to the organelles found in animal cells.
  • Cells specialise through differentiation — most animal cells differentiate early, but plant cells can differentiate throughout life via meristems.
  • Electron microscopes have far higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes, enabling scientists to see sub-cellular detail.
  • The magnification formula is \(\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}\) — always convert to the same units first.

lessons.title: Cell Division and Transport
lessons.description: How cells divide by mitosis and meiosis, plus osmosis, diffusion and active transport.
lessons.content_html:
The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

Cells in your body divide to grow, repair damaged tissue and replace worn-out cells. This process follows a pattern called the cell cycle. Most of the cell cycle is spent in a growth phase called interphase, during which the cell’s DNA is replicated and the number of sub-cellular structures (organelles) increases.

Once the cell has copied all of its DNA and organelles, it enters mitosis. During mitosis, one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell. The cytoplasm and cell membrane then divide to produce two genetically identical daughter cells. Each daughter cell has the full set of 46 chromosomes (in humans).

Key Fact

Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell. It is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. The cell cycle consists of interphase (growth + DNA replication) followed by mitosis and cell division.

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and become specialised. In humans, embryonic stem cells can differentiate into almost any cell type, while adult stem cells (found in bone marrow) are more limited. In plants, meristem tissue retains the ability to differentiate throughout the plant’s life.

Stem cells have therapeutic uses — for example, treating paralysis or diabetes — but raise ethical concerns, particularly around the use of embryonic stem cells. You need to be able to discuss both the potential benefits and the ethical objections.

Diffusion

Diffusion is the spreading out of particles from a region where they are at a higher concentration to a region where they are at a lower concentration. It occurs in both liquids and gases and does not require energy. Oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out of cells by diffusion.

The rate of diffusion is affected by the concentration gradient (a steeper gradient means faster diffusion), the temperature (higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy), the surface area of the membrane and the distance the particles must travel.

Key Fact

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration. It is a passive process (no energy required). Factors affecting rate: concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance.

Osmosis

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution (high water concentration) to a more concentrated solution (low water concentration). Like diffusion, osmosis is a passive process.

In Required Practical 3, you investigate the effect of a range of sugar solutions on the mass of plant tissue. Potato cylinders placed in distilled water gain mass (water enters cells by osmosis) while those in concentrated sugar solution lose mass (water leaves cells).

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration. This requires energy from cellular respiration. Examples include root hair cells absorbing mineral ions from the soil and the absorption of sugar from the gut into the blood.

Active transport is essential when a cell needs to accumulate substances at a higher concentration than the surrounding environment. The energy for this process comes from the mitochondria.

Comparing Transport Methods

A common exam question asks you to compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport. Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy needed) and move substances down the concentration gradient. Active transport requires energy and moves substances against the concentration gradient. Osmosis specifically describes the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing transport processes, always state the direction of movement relative to the concentration gradient. For a 6-mark question, structure your answer clearly: name the process, state the direction, whether energy is required, and give a biological example for each.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical cells for growth and repair; the cell cycle includes interphase and mitosis.
  • Diffusion moves particles from high to low concentration (passive); osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane.
  • Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient and requires energy from respiration.

lessons.title: Organisation and the Digestive System
lessons.description: From cells to organ systems, with a focus on how the digestive system breaks down food.
lessons.content_html:
Levels of Organisation

The human body is organised into a hierarchy. Individual cells with a similar structure and function are grouped together into tissues. Different tissues combine to form organs, and organs work together as organ systems. The digestive system is one of the main organ systems you need to know.

Key Fact

The hierarchy of organisation: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism. Each level builds on the one below it.

The Digestive System

The digestive system is a muscular tube running from the mouth to the anus. Its role is to break large, insoluble food molecules into smaller, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. Digestion involves both mechanical breakdown (teeth, churning in the stomach) and chemical breakdown by enzymes.

The main digestive enzymes are:

  • Amylase — produced in the salivary glands and pancreas; breaks down starch into sugars (maltose).
  • Proteases — produced in the stomach (pepsin), pancreas and small intestine; break down proteins into amino acids.
  • Lipases — produced in the pancreas and small intestine; break down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.

Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the small intestine where it has two key functions: it neutralises the hydrochloric acid from the stomach (creating alkaline conditions for enzymes in the small intestine) and it emulsifies fats — breaking large fat droplets into smaller ones to increase the surface area for lipase to work on.

Key Fact

Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and emulsifies fats in the small intestine. It also neutralises stomach acid to create the alkaline conditions needed by intestinal enzymes.

Enzymes and the Lock-and-Key Model

Enzymes are biological catalysts — they speed up reactions without being used up. Each enzyme has a specific active site with a unique shape. Only a substrate with the matching shape can fit into the active site, like a key in a lock. This is called the lock-and-key model.

Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature and pH. If the temperature is too high or the pH is too extreme, the active site changes shape (denaturation) and the substrate can no longer fit. The enzyme stops working.

You should know the food tests for AQA Required Practical 2:

  • Starch — Iodine solution turns from brown-orange to blue-black.
  • Sugars — Benedict’s reagent heated; turns from blue to green/yellow/orange/red (depending on sugar concentration).
  • Proteins — Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple/lilac.
  • Lipids — Sudan III test; a red layer forms if lipids are present.

The digestive system demonstrates how organs work together as a system. The stomach churns food and adds acid; the pancreas produces enzymes; the liver makes bile; the small intestine absorbs soluble products into the blood; and the large intestine absorbs water.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common 6-mark question asks you to describe the role of enzymes in digestion. Structure your answer by enzyme type: name the enzyme, state where it is produced, what it breaks down, and what the products are. Don’t forget bile — it is not an enzyme but plays a key role.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The body is organised: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.
  • Digestive enzymes (amylase, proteases, lipases) break large molecules into smaller soluble ones for absorption.
  • Enzymes have a specific active site shape (lock-and-key model) and are denatured by high temperature or extreme pH.

practice_questions.text: Describe the journey of a starch molecule through the digestive system, from the mouth to absorption.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed, logical account covering mechanical and chemical digestion.
Starch enters the mouth where it is mechanically broken down by teeth (1). Amylase in saliva begins to break starch into maltose/sugars (1). Food passes to the stomach where acid provides conditions for protease (pepsin) but amylase is denatured (1). In the small intestine, pancreatic amylase continues to break down remaining starch into sugars (1). Bile from the liver neutralises stomach acid to create alkaline conditions for intestinal enzymes (1). The small, soluble sugar molecules are absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the bloodstream (1).

lessons.title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease
lessons.description: The structure of the heart, blood vessels and blood, plus coronary heart disease treatments.
lessons.content_html:
The Heart

The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood around the body through a double circulatory system. The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circuit). The left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body (systemic circuit).

The heart has four chambers: two upper atria (singular: atrium) that receive blood, and two lower ventricles that pump blood out. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right because it needs to generate higher pressure to pump blood around the entire body, whereas the right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs.

Key Fact

The heart has four chambers. Blood flows: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

Valves in the heart prevent the backflow of blood. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with the oxygenated blood it needs to keep beating.

Blood Vessels

There are three types of blood vessel:

  • Arteries — carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, muscular, elastic walls.
  • Veins — carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls and contain valves to prevent backflow.
  • Capillaries — tiny vessels that connect arteries to veins. Their walls are one cell thick, allowing efficient exchange of substances (oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide) with body tissues.

Blood Components

Blood is a tissue made up of four components:

  • Red blood cells — contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen. They have a biconcave disc shape to increase surface area and no nucleus to carry more haemoglobin.
  • White blood cells — part of the immune system. Phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies.
  • Platelets — cell fragments that help blood to clot at wound sites, forming a scab to prevent blood loss and infection.
  • Plasma — the liquid part of blood. It transports dissolved substances including carbon dioxide, urea, hormones and glucose.

Coronary heart disease (CHD) occurs when layers of fatty material (atheroma) build up inside the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. This can cause a heart attack if the heart muscle does not receive enough oxygen.

Treatments include: stents (wire mesh tubes inserted to hold the artery open), statins (drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels and slow the build-up of fatty deposits), and in severe cases, heart transplants or artificial hearts (mechanical devices that keep blood flowing while waiting for a transplant).

Key Fact

Coronary heart disease is caused by fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries. Treatments include stents (hold arteries open), statins (lower cholesterol), heart transplants and artificial hearts.

Stents are effective but carry risks of infection and blood clots. Statins must be taken long-term and can cause side effects such as headaches and muscle pain. Artificial hearts are temporary and can cause blood clots or infection. Heart transplants are limited by donor availability and the risk of rejection by the immune system.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to compare arteries, veins and capillaries, structure your answer as a table in your head: wall thickness, lumen size, valves, blood pressure. Always link structure to function — e.g. capillaries have thin walls to allow efficient diffusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The heart pumps blood through a double circulatory system; the left ventricle has a thicker wall to generate higher pressure.
  • Arteries have thick walls (high pressure), veins have valves (low pressure), capillaries are one cell thick (for exchange).
  • Coronary heart disease is treated with stents, statins, or heart transplants/artificial hearts.

lessons.title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues
lessons.description: Risk factors for non-communicable diseases, cancer, and how plant tissues are organised.
lessons.content_html:
Health and Disease

Health is a state of physical and mental wellbeing. Disease is a condition where part of the body does not function properly. Diseases can be communicable (caused by pathogens and spread between people) or non-communicable (not caused by pathogens and cannot be passed on). Sometimes diseases interact — for example, immune system conditions can make a person more susceptible to communicable diseases.

Key Fact

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are not caused by pathogens and cannot be spread. Major NCDs include cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, lung disease and cancer. Risk factors include smoking, obesity, alcohol and lack of exercise.

Risk Factors for Non-Communicable Diseases

A risk factor is something that increases the probability of developing a disease. Key risk factors include:

  • Smoking — linked to lung cancer, cardiovascular disease and lung disease.
  • Obesity — a risk factor for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
  • Alcohol — linked to liver disease and some cancers.
  • Lack of exercise — increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and obesity.

It is important to understand the difference between a risk factor and a cause. Risk factors are correlated with disease — they make disease more likely — but correlation does not always prove causation.

Cancer is caused by changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division. Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells contained in one area — they do not invade other tissues. Malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissues and can spread to other parts of the body through the blood, forming secondary tumours — this is known as metastasis.

Risk factors for cancer include genetic factors, ionising radiation (e.g. UV light), certain viruses (e.g. HPV), and lifestyle factors such as smoking and obesity.

Plant Tissues and Organ Systems

Plants are also organised into tissues and organs. The main plant tissues include:

  • Epidermal tissue — covers the surface of the plant for protection.
  • Palisade mesophyll — packed with chloroplasts and located near the top of the leaf where it receives the most light for photosynthesis.
  • Spongy mesophyll — has air spaces that allow gases (\(CO_2\) and \(O_2\)) to diffuse easily.
  • Xylem — xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves. It is made of hollow, dead cells with lignified walls.
  • Phloem — phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant in a process called translocation.
Key Fact

Xylem transports water and minerals upwards (transpiration stream). Phloem transports dissolved sugars to where they are needed (translocation). Xylem cells are dead and hollow; phloem cells are living.

Transpiration is the evaporation and diffusion of water from the surface of leaves, mainly through the stomata. This creates a continuous transpiration stream that pulls water up through the xylem from the roots. The rate of transpiration is affected by temperature, humidity, air movement and light intensity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked about risk factors, always use the word “increases the risk of” rather than “causes” — unless the question specifically asks about causation. Also be prepared to compare benign and malignant tumours in terms of invasion and metastasis.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Non-communicable diseases (cancer, CHD, type 2 diabetes) are linked to risk factors like smoking, obesity and alcohol — but risk factors don’t always prove causation.
  • Malignant tumours invade other tissues and can metastasise; benign tumours stay in one place.
  • Plants have specialised tissues: xylem (water transport), phloem (sugar transport), palisade mesophyll (photosynthesis).

lessons.title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences
lessons.description: Covers what are communicable diseases?, types of pathogens, how diseases spread and more.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Communicable Diseases?

Communicable diseases are illnesses that can be spread from one organism to another. They are caused by pathogens — harmful microorganisms that invade the body and cause infection.

Key Fact

There are four main types of pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protists. Each type causes disease in different ways and requires different treatments.

Types of Pathogens

Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can reproduce rapidly inside the body. Some bacteria cause disease by producing toxins that damage tissues. Examples include food poisoning (Salmonella) and gonorrhoea (a sexually transmitted infection).

Bacterial infections can be treated with antibiotics, which kill bacteria or stop them from reproducing.

Viruses are not cells — they are much smaller than bacteria and can only reproduce inside living cells. They take over the cell’s machinery to make copies of themselves, often destroying the cell in the process. Examples include measles, HIV, and tobacco mosaic virus in plants.

Viral infections cannot be treated with antibiotics. Instead, the body’s immune system must fight them off, though antiviral drugs can help in some cases.

Fungi and protists are the other two types of pathogens. Fungi like athlete’s foot affect the skin, while protists such as the malaria parasite are often spread by vectors like mosquitoes.

How Diseases Spread

Pathogens can be transmitted (spread) between organisms in several ways:

  • Air: Droplets containing pathogens are released when infected people cough, sneeze, or talk. These can be breathed in by others.
  • Water: Contaminated water can contain pathogens that cause diseases like cholera.
  • Direct contact: Some diseases spread through touching infected surfaces or direct skin contact.
  • Vectors: Animals like mosquitoes can carry pathogens from one host to another.
Key Fact

The spread of communicable diseases can be reduced by hygiene measures, destroying vectors, isolation of infected individuals, and vaccination.

The Body’s Defence Systems

The human body has evolved several defence mechanisms to protect against pathogens. These work as barriers to prevent pathogens entering, or as immune responses to destroy them once inside.

Non-Specific Defences

The body’s first line of defence includes physical and chemical barriers:

  • Skin: Acts as a physical barrier to prevent pathogens entering the body
  • Nose: Contains hairs and mucus that trap particles and pathogens
  • Trachea and bronchi: Lined with cells that produce mucus to trap pathogens, and have cilia that sweep mucus upward
  • Stomach: Produces hydrochloric acid that kills many pathogens in food and drink

The Immune System

If pathogens get past the body’s barriers, the immune system provides the second line of defence. This involves white blood cells that can detect and destroy pathogens.

Phagocytosis: Some white blood cells engulf and digest pathogens. This is a non-specific response that works against any pathogen.

Antibody production: Other white blood cells produce antibodies. These are proteins that bind to specific antigens on the surface of pathogens.

Antitoxin production: White blood cells can also produce antitoxins that neutralise the toxins released by some bacteria.

Memory Cells and Immunity

When white blood cells encounter a pathogen for the first time, some become memory cells. These remain in the blood for many years and provide immunity.

If the same pathogen enters the body again, memory cells quickly recognise it and produce antibodies much faster than the first time. This rapid response often prevents symptoms of disease from developing — the person is immune.

Primary response: When first exposed to a pathogen, it takes several days for white blood cells to recognise it and start producing the right antibodies. During this time, the person may become ill.

Secondary response: Memory cells enable a much faster and stronger antibody response on second exposure. This usually prevents illness.

Vaccination

Vaccination involves introducing small amounts of dead or inactive pathogens into the body. This stimulates white blood cells to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing disease.

If the person is later infected with the live pathogen, their memory cells will recognise it and quickly produce antibodies. This provides immunity without having to suffer from the disease first.

Key Fact

Vaccination programmes have successfully reduced the incidence of many diseases. However, vaccines need to be updated regularly for diseases like flu because the pathogens mutate and change their antigens.

Antibiotics and Drug Resistance

Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them reproducing. They have dramatically reduced deaths from bacterial infections since their discovery. However, antibiotics do not work against viruses.

The overuse and misuse of antibiotics has led to the evolution of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. These “superbugs” are difficult to treat and pose a serious threat to human health.

To slow the development of antibiotic resistance:

  • Doctors should only prescribe antibiotics for bacterial infections
  • Patients must complete the full course of antibiotics, even if they feel better
  • New antibiotics need to be developed to replace those that no longer work
lessons.exam_tip_html: Exam questions often ask you to explain the difference between bacteria and viruses, or to describe how white blood cells fight disease. Remember that antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses, and that memory cells provide the link between vaccination and immunity. Draw diagrams to show phagocytosis and antibody-antigen binding if asked.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Communicable diseases are caused by four types of pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists
  • The body defends itself using physical barriers and the immune system with white blood cells
  • Memory cells provide immunity by enabling rapid antibody production on second exposure to a pathogen
  • Vaccination creates immunity safely, while antibiotic resistance threatens our ability to treat bacterial infections

lessons.title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development
lessons.description: How vaccines and antibiotics work, antibiotic resistance, and the stages of drug testing.
lessons.content_html:
Vaccination

A vaccination introduces a small quantity of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body. This stimulates the white blood cells (lymphocytes) to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen enters the body again in the future, the white blood cells can respond rapidly and produce the correct antibodies much faster, preventing infection.

Key Fact

Vaccines stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies by introducing dead or weakened pathogens. Memory lymphocytes remain, allowing a rapid secondary immune response if the pathogen is encountered again.

If a large proportion of the population is vaccinated, the spread of the pathogen is greatly reduced because there are fewer people who can become infected and pass it on. This is called herd immunity.

Antibiotics and Painkillers

Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or prevent them from reproducing inside the body. They are used to treat bacterial infections. Antibiotics do not work on viruses because viruses reproduce inside the host’s own cells, and it is very difficult to damage the virus without also damaging the host cell.

Painkillers treat the symptoms of disease (e.g. pain, inflammation) but do not kill pathogens. They make the patient feel better but do not cure the infection itself.

Some bacteria have developed antibiotic resistance through natural selection. Mutations in bacterial DNA can produce strains that are not killed by an antibiotic. These resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance gene. Overuse of antibiotics and failure to complete courses accelerates this process.

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is an example of a “superbug” that is resistant to several antibiotics. To reduce the development of resistant strains, doctors should only prescribe antibiotics when necessary, patients should always complete the full course, and the agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted.

Drug Development and Testing

New drugs must go through rigorous testing before they can be used. The stages are:

Stage 1 — Preclinical testing: The drug is tested on cells, tissues and live animals. This checks for toxicity (is it safe?), efficacy (does it work?) and dose (how much is needed?).

Stage 2 — Clinical trials: If preclinical tests are successful, the drug is tested on healthy volunteers and then on patients. A very low dose is given first to check for side effects. Double-blind trials are used where neither the patient nor the doctor knows who receives the real drug and who receives a placebo (an inactive substance). This eliminates bias.

Stage 3 — Peer review and approval: Results are reviewed by independent scientists and regulatory bodies before the drug is approved for widespread use.

Key Fact

Drug testing stages: preclinical (cells, tissues, animals) → clinical trials (healthy volunteers, then patients, using double-blind placebo trials) → peer review and approval. This process typically takes over 10 years.

Many drugs were originally discovered in plants or microorganisms. For example, the painkiller aspirin was originally derived from willow bark, the heart drug digitalis comes from foxgloves, and the antibiotic penicillin was discovered from a mould by Alexander Fleming in 1928.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A very common exam question asks why antibiotics cannot be used to treat viral infections. The key point is that viruses reproduce inside host cells, so any drug that kills the virus would also damage the host cell. Make sure you can also explain the stages of clinical trials and the purpose of placebos and double-blind testing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Vaccines introduce dead/weakened pathogens to stimulate antibody production and create immune memory.
  • Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses; overuse leads to antibiotic resistance through natural selection.
  • New drugs go through preclinical testing (animals/cells), clinical trials (double-blind, placebo-controlled) and peer review.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration
lessons.description: The equations and limiting factors for photosynthesis, plus aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
lessons.content_html:
Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction that takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells. It uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. The word equation is:

$$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$

The balanced symbol equation is:

$$6CO_2 + 6H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{light}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$$

Key Fact

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). It takes place in the chloroplasts and requires light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.

The rate of photosynthesis is affected by three limiting factors:

  • Light intensity — as light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases until another factor becomes limiting.
  • Carbon dioxide concentration — increasing \(CO_2\) increases the rate until another factor limits it.
  • Temperature — higher temperatures increase the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions up to an optimum, beyond which enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply.

These limiting factors interact, and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis at a given time. Light intensity follows an inverse square law — it is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source: \(\text{light intensity} \propto \frac{1}{d^2}\). You may need to explain graphs of photosynthesis rate involving two or three limiting factors simultaneously.

Plants use the glucose produced during photosynthesis for several purposes: respiration (to release energy), converting glucose to starch for storage, producing cellulose for cell walls, producing amino acids (by combining with nitrate ions from the soil) for protein synthesis, and producing lipids (fats and oils) for storage in seeds.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration is an exothermic reaction that takes place continuously in all living cells. It occurs in the mitochondria and requires oxygen. The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$$

The balanced symbol equation is:

$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O$$

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\). It is exothermic, occurs in mitochondria, and releases energy for life processes including muscle contraction, maintaining body temperature and building molecules.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is not available. It releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration because glucose is only partially broken down.

In animals: \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}\)

In plants and yeast (fermentation): \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}\)

During intense exercise, the muscles cannot get enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, so anaerobic respiration occurs alongside it. This produces lactic acid, which builds up in the muscles and causes fatigue and cramp. After exercise, you continue to breathe heavily to repay the oxygen debt — the extra oxygen needed to break down the accumulated lactic acid.

Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.

During exercise, the body responds to the increased demand for energy: heart rate increases, breathing rate and depth increase, and blood is redirected to the muscles. These changes supply more oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration and remove more carbon dioxide.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Make sure you can write both the word and symbol equations for photosynthesis and respiration. A common mistake is confusing which is endothermic and which is exothermic. Remember: photosynthesis takes in energy (endothermic), respiration releases energy (exothermic). For limiting factors questions, always explain why the graph plateaus.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Photosynthesis is endothermic (in chloroplasts): \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). Limited by light, \(CO_2\) and temperature.
  • Aerobic respiration is exothermic (in mitochondria): \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\).
  • Anaerobic respiration releases less energy; in animals it produces lactic acid, in yeast it produces ethanol + \(CO_2\).

lessons.title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease
lessons.description: How scientists grow bacteria safely and how pathogens attack plants.
lessons.content_html:
Culturing Microorganisms

Microorganisms such as bacteria can be grown in the laboratory using nutrient media. This allows scientists to study how they grow, test antibiotics, and investigate disease. In the separate biology specification, you need to understand the practical techniques used to culture microorganisms safely and aseptically.

Key Fact

An aseptic technique is used to prevent contamination of bacterial cultures by unwanted microorganisms from the environment. This ensures that only the microorganism being studied grows on the culture medium.

To culture bacteria, scientists use either a nutrient agar plate or a nutrient broth. Agar plates provide a solid surface on which individual colonies can be seen, while broth allows bacteria to grow in liquid suspension.

Aseptic Technique Steps

To prevent contamination, a specific set of precautions must be followed during any work with microorganisms:

  • Sterilise all equipment (Petri dishes, inoculating loops) before use — an inoculating loop is passed through a Bunsen burner flame until it glows red.
  • Lids of Petri dishes are secured with tape but not sealed completely, to allow oxygen in but prevent contamination from above.
  • Work near a Bunsen flame to create an updraught that carries airborne microorganisms away from the open plates.
  • Incubate cultures at a maximum of 25 °C in schools (to reduce the risk of growing pathogens harmful to humans). In industry, cultures can be incubated at higher temperatures, often around 37 °C.

You may be asked to describe how to investigate the effect of antiseptics or antibiotics on bacterial growth. Paper discs soaked in different concentrations of antiseptic are placed on an inoculated agar plate. After incubation, clear zones called zones of inhibition show where bacteria could not grow.

The area of the zone of inhibition can be calculated using \(A = \pi r^2\), where \(r\) is the radius of the clear zone. A larger zone means the antiseptic is more effective at killing or preventing bacterial growth.

Plant Disease

Plants can be infected by a range of pathogens including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and protists. These diseases reduce crop yields and can devastate agriculture. You need to know specific examples and how to identify diseased plants.

Key Fact

Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) causes a mosaic pattern on leaves, reducing the area available for photosynthesis. There is no cure — infected plants must be destroyed.

Examples of Plant Diseases

Rose black spot is a fungal disease that causes purple or black spots on leaves. Affected leaves turn yellow and drop early, reducing the plant’s ability to photosynthesise. It spreads through water and wind and can be treated with fungicides or by removing and destroying affected leaves.

Crown gall disease is caused by the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, which inserts its DNA into the plant cells and causes tumour-like growths (galls) on stems and roots.

Plant diseases can be identified by:

  • Stunted growth — nutrient deficiency or pathogen infection.
  • Spots on leaves — fungal or bacterial infection (e.g. rose black spot).
  • Areas of decay or rot — fungal or bacterial infection.
  • Discolouration — viral infection (e.g. TMV mosaic pattern) or mineral deficiency.
  • Malformed stems or leaves — viral infection or pest damage.

Gardeners and farmers can also use testing kits, laboratory analysis, or reference material to confirm diagnoses.

Plant Defence Responses

Plants have evolved physical, chemical, and mechanical defences against pathogens and herbivores:

  • Physical barriers: Cellulose cell walls, tough waxy cuticles on leaves, and bark on trees prevent pathogen entry.
  • Chemical defences: Some plants produce antimicrobial substances (e.g. mint and witch hazel) or poisons to deter herbivores.
  • Mechanical adaptations: Thorns, hairs, and leaves that droop or curl when touched deter herbivores.
Key Fact

Plants cannot move away from threats, so their defences must be structural or chemical. Some plants seal off infected areas by producing callose deposits to block the spread of pathogens through the phloem.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to calculate the area of a zone of inhibition, always measure the diameter first, then halve it to find the radius before applying \(A = \pi r^2\). Show your working clearly and give units (mm²). Exam questions on aseptic technique often ask you to explain why each step is necessary — link every step to preventing contamination.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Aseptic technique prevents contamination when culturing microorganisms — sterilise equipment, work near a flame, and incubate at a maximum of 25 °C in schools.
  • Plants can be infected by viruses (TMV), fungi (rose black spot), bacteria, and protists — symptoms include spots, discolouration, and stunted growth.
  • Plants defend themselves with physical barriers (cell walls, cuticle), chemical defences (antimicrobial compounds), and mechanical adaptations (thorns).

lessons.title: Monoclonal Antibodies
lessons.description: How monoclonal antibodies are produced and their uses in medicine and research.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Monoclonal Antibodies?

Monoclonal antibodies are identical copies of one specific antibody. They are produced from a single clone of cells, so every antibody molecule is exactly the same and binds to the same specific antigen. This makes them extremely useful in medicine and research.

Key Fact

Monoclonal antibodies are produced by stimulating mouse lymphocytes to make a specific antibody, then fusing those lymphocytes with tumour cells to create hybridoma cells that divide indefinitely and produce large quantities of the desired antibody.

Producing Monoclonal Antibodies

The production of monoclonal antibodies is a multi-step process:

  1. A mouse is injected with the target antigen. Its immune system responds by producing lymphocytes that make antibodies against that antigen.
  2. The antibody-producing lymphocytes are collected from the mouse’s spleen.
  3. These lymphocytes are fused with tumour cells (which divide rapidly and indefinitely) to form hybridoma cells.
  4. The hybridoma cells are screened to select those that produce the correct antibody.
  5. Selected hybridoma cells are cloned and grown in large quantities. They produce vast amounts of the identical monoclonal antibody.

Normal lymphocytes die after a short time outside the body. Tumour cells, however, divide uncontrollably and can survive indefinitely in culture. By fusing a lymphocyte (which makes the right antibody) with a tumour cell (which can divide forever), scientists create a hybridoma that combines both properties — it produces the correct antibody and never stops dividing.

Uses of Monoclonal Antibodies

Because monoclonal antibodies bind to one specific antigen with very high precision, they have a wide range of applications:

Pregnancy Testing

HCG (human chorionic gonadotrophin) is a hormone produced during pregnancy. Pregnancy test sticks contain monoclonal antibodies that bind to HCG in urine. If HCG is present, the antibodies trigger a colour change, producing a positive result.

Diagnosis of Disease

Monoclonal antibodies can detect specific molecules in blood or tissue samples. For example, they can identify the presence of a pathogen or a specific protein linked to a disease. In cancer diagnosis, monoclonal antibodies labelled with a radioactive tracer or fluorescent dye can bind to tumour-specific antigens, allowing doctors to locate tumours in the body through imaging.

Key Fact

In cancer treatment, monoclonal antibodies can be designed to carry a toxic drug, radioactive substance, or chemical directly to cancer cells. This is targeted therapy — it delivers the treatment only to the tumour, reducing damage to healthy tissue compared with chemotherapy.

Scientists use monoclonal antibodies to locate and identify specific molecules in cells and tissues. They can be tagged with fluorescent dyes, allowing researchers to visualise exactly where a particular protein is within a cell. This technique is invaluable in laboratory research for understanding cell biology and disease mechanisms.

Limitations and Ethical Concerns

Monoclonal antibodies were expected to be more widely used than they currently are. There are limitations:

  • They can cause unexpected side effects in some patients, which are sometimes more severe than the disease itself.
  • They are expensive to develop and produce.
  • They do not yet produce the miracle cures that were initially hoped for.

There are also ethical concerns about the use of animals (mice) in the production process, as mice must be injected with antigens to stimulate antibody production.

Key Fact

Monoclonal antibody treatment is an example of targeted therapy because it delivers drugs precisely to diseased cells while leaving healthy cells unharmed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on monoclonal antibodies often ask you to describe the production process — learn the five steps in order. A common mistake is confusing hybridoma cells with normal lymphocytes. Remember: hybridoma = lymphocyte + tumour cell. If asked to evaluate their use, balance benefits (specificity, targeted treatment) against limitations (side effects, cost, ethical concerns about animal use).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies produced by hybridoma cells (lymphocyte fused with a tumour cell).
  • They are used in pregnancy tests (detecting HCG), disease diagnosis, cancer treatment (targeted drug delivery), and research.
  • Limitations include side effects, high cost, and ethical concerns about using mice in production.

practice_questions.text: Explain why tumour cells are used in the production of monoclonal antibodies.
practice_questions.marks: Tumour cells can divide indefinitely/are immortal (1 mark). Normal lymphocytes die after a short time (1 mark). Fusing them creates hybridoma cells that can divide indefinitely AND produce the desired antibody (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Compare the use of monoclonal antibodies in cancer treatment with the use of conventional chemotherapy.
practice_questions.marks: Monoclonal antibodies target specific cancer cells/antigens (1 mark) while chemotherapy affects all rapidly dividing cells, including healthy ones (1 mark). Monoclonal antibodies cause fewer side effects to healthy tissue (1 mark) but are more expensive to produce and may still cause unexpected side effects (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Monoclonal antibodies have many potential uses in medicine. Evaluate the benefits and limitations of using monoclonal antibodies for the treatment and diagnosis of disease.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed evaluation covering both treatment and diagnosis, with specific examples, clear benefits and limitations, and a reasoned conclusion.
Mid band (3-4): Describes benefits and limitations of monoclonal antibodies with some examples. May cover treatment or diagnosis but not both in detail.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements about uses or limitations without detail.
Indicative content:
• Benefits in diagnosis: detect specific antigens on pathogens/cancer cells; used with fluorescent dyes/radioactive tracers for imaging; pregnancy tests detect HCG quickly and cheaply
• Benefits in treatment: targeted drug delivery to cancer cells; less damage to healthy tissue than chemotherapy; can carry toxic drugs or radioactive substances directly to tumour
• Limitations: can produce unexpected side effects, sometimes severe; expensive to develop and produce; ethical issues with mouse use; have not produced the widespread cures once hoped for
• Conclusion should weigh benefits against limitations
